heading: 1. 39.8% of Metal-Important Genes Are Also NaCl-Important

text: The pooled overlap was 4,304/10,821 metal-important gene records (39.8%) across 19 organisms, 14 metals, and 86 organism × metal pairs. This pooled percentage is distinct from the per-metal organism-level means.
quote: Across 19 organisms and 14 metals (86 organism × metal pairs), 4,304 of 10,821 metal-important gene records (39.8%) are also important under NaCl stress. This substantial overlap exists for every metal tested — from 9.2% for molybdenum to 57.6% for manganese — indicating that a large fraction of the "metal fitness" signal reflects general cellular vulnerability shared between metal and osmotic/ionic stress.
heading: 1. 39.8% of Metal-Important Genes Are Also NaCl-Important

text: Synechococcus elongatus (SynE) had 88.6% shared-stress genes (565/638) and 12 NaCl experiments spanning 0.5–250 mM, versus 1–6 experiments elsewhere. Excluding it reduced pooled overlap from 39.8% to 36.7% (3,739/10,183); the n_sick >= 1 rule is easier to meet with more experiments.
quote: **Sensitivity to outliers**: *Synechococcus elongatus* (SynE) is a dramatic outlier at 88.6% shared-stress (565/638 genes), driven by its 12 NaCl dose-response experiments spanning 0.5–250 mM — far more than any other organism (1–6 NaCl experiments). The `n_sick >= 1` threshold is much easier to satisfy with 12 experiments. Excluding SynE, the overall overlap drops modestly from 39.8% to 36.7% (3,739/10,183), confirming that the finding is not driven by this outlier. The next-highest organisms (Korea 58.6%, Phaeo 56.4%, Pedo557 53.0%) have typical NaCl experiment counts.
heading: 1. 39.8% of Metal-Important Genes Are Also NaCl-Important

heading: 2. Counter Ions Are NOT the Primary Driver of the Overlap

text: The report found no chloride-dose pattern: zinc sulfate at 0 mM Cl⁻ had 44.6% NaCl overlap, versus cobalt 41.3% (up to 500 mM Cl⁻), copper 41.0%, and nickel 39.3%. It reports group means of 41.6% for chloride metals and 37.8% for non-chloride metals; the biological explanation is interpretive.
quote: The critical test: does the overlap scale with chloride delivered by the metal salt? **No.** Zinc sulfate (0 mM Cl⁻) shows 44.6% NaCl overlap — higher than most chloride-delivered metals including cobalt (41.3%, up to 500 mM Cl⁻), copper (41.0%), and nickel (39.3%). Chloride metals as a group (mean 41.6%) are barely different from non-chloride metals (37.8%). The overlap is driven by shared stress biology — cell envelope damage, ion homeostasis disruption, and general stress response — not by chloride counter ions.
heading: 2. Counter Ions Are NOT the Primary Driver of the Overlap

text: Figure reference: DvH metal-fitness profile correlations with NaCl, figures/dvh_nacl_metal_correlation.png.
quote: ![DvH fitness profile correlations with NaCl](figures/dvh_nacl_metal_correlation.png)
heading: 3. DvH Metal-NaCl Correlation Follows Toxicity Mechanism, Not Chloride Dose

text: In DvH, profiled with 13 metals and 6 NaCl experiments, whole-genome metal–NaCl fitness correlations ranged from zinc r=0.715 to iron r=0.086. Zinc ranked first despite sulfate delivery and zero Cl⁻; the toxicity-mechanism explanation is interpretive.
quote: In DvH (the most extensively profiled organism: 13 metals, 6 NaCl experiments), whole-genome fitness correlations between each metal and NaCl reveal a hierarchy: Zinc (r=0.715) > Manganese (0.545) > Copper (0.532) > Cobalt (0.498) > Mercury (0.478) > Nickel (0.446) > Aluminum (0.420) > Molybdenum (0.396) > Uranium (0.350) > Selenium (0.342) > Chromium (0.318) > Tungsten (0.298) > Iron (0.086). This hierarchy does not follow Cl⁻ concentration (zinc is delivered as sulfate with zero Cl⁻ but ranks first). Instead, it follows toxicity mechanism: metals that broadly displace essential cofactors (Zn, Mn, Cu, Co) share more genes with NaCl stress than metals that target specific pathways (Mo, W — molybdopterin enzymes; Fe — iron-sulfur clusters).
heading: 3. DvH Metal-NaCl Correlation Follows Toxicity Mechanism, Not Chloride Dose

quote: ![Original vs corrected core enrichment per metal](figures/atlas_original_vs_corrected.png)
heading: 4. Metal Fitness Atlas Core Enrichment Is Robust After Correction

text: The narrative says core enrichment was preserved for 12 of 14 metals and that only cadmium reversed. It reports increased deltas for molybdenum (+0.132 → +0.145), tungsten (+0.129 → +0.134), mercury (+0.116 → +0.133), and selenium (+0.115 → +0.131), but decreased deltas for aluminum (+0.099 → +0.068) and zinc (+0.145 → +0.115). Its reversal wording conflicts with the corrected-conservation table: cadmium remains negative, while iron changes sign.
quote: After removing the ~40% shared-stress genes and restricting to metal-specific genes, the core genome enrichment is fully preserved for 12 of 14 metals. Essential metals actually show **stronger** enrichment after correction: Molybdenum (delta +0.132 → +0.145), Tungsten (+0.129 → +0.134), Mercury (+0.116 → +0.133), Selenium (+0.115 → +0.131). Toxic metals with broad cellular effects show modest decreases: Aluminum (+0.099 → +0.068), Zinc (+0.145 → +0.115). Only Cadmium reverses (delta -0.008 → -0.108), but with only 92 original genes from 1 organism, this has very low statistical power. The original atlas conclusion — metal fitness genes are core-enriched — is not an artifact of shared stress response overlap.
heading: 4. Metal Fitness Atlas Core Enrichment Is Robust After Correction

quote: ![Per-metal gene classification: shared-stress vs metal-specific](figures/gene_classification_by_metal.png)
heading: 5. Gene Classification: 60% of Metal Fitness Genes Are Metal-Specific

text: Of 10,821 metal-important gene records, 6,517 (60.2%) were classified as metal-specific. In DvH, 495 unique genes comprised 73 shared-stress (14.7%) and 422 metal-specific (85.3%); shared-stress genes were important for a mean 4.1 metals versus 2.5, and SEED annotation coverage was 78.1% versus 90.5%, respectively. Functional interpretations are descriptive.
quote: Across all organisms, 6,517 of 10,821 metal-important gene records (60.2%) are classified as metal-specific (important for metals but not NaCl). For DvH, 495 unique metal-important genes split into 73 shared-stress (14.7%) and 422 metal-specific (85.3%). Shared-stress genes tend to be important across more metals (mean 4.1 metals per gene vs 2.5 for metal-specific), consistent with broad cellular vulnerability. In DvH, metal-specific genes are more functionally annotated (90.5% have SEED annotations) than shared-stress genes (78.1%), suggesting that the metal-specific set includes well-characterized metal homeostasis functions (Ni/Fe-hydrogenase, nitrogenase regulators, metal transporters) while shared-stress genes include more uncharacterized general stress proteins.
heading: 5. Gene Classification: 60% of Metal Fitness Genes Are Metal-Specific

heading: 6. psRCH2: The Only Within-Metal Counter Ion Comparison

text: psRCH2 supplied the only within-metal counter-ion comparison: copper as CuCl₂ (anaerobic, 3 replicates) and CuSO₄ (aerobic, 3 replicates). Cross-salt fitness correlation was r=0.439, versus within-replicate correlations of r=0.720 and r=0.859.

text: The psRCH2 copper-salt comparison cannot isolate counter-ion effects because the salts were tested under different oxygen conditions.
quote: However, this comparison is severely confounded by aerobic/anaerobic growth — hundreds of genes differ between these conditions independent of copper.
heading: 6. psRCH2: The Only Within-Metal Counter Ion Comparison

text: In psRCH2, aerobic CuSO₄ without Cl⁻ correlated more strongly with NaCl (r=0.450) than anaerobic CuCl₂ did (r=0.212), but the growth-condition confound limits attribution to counter ions.
quote: Notably, CuSO₄ (aerobic, no Cl⁻) is more correlated with NaCl (r=0.450) than CuCl₂ (anaerobic, r=0.212), further arguing against chloride as the primary confound and suggesting the aerobic/NaCl correlation reflects shared aerobic stress mechanisms.
heading: 6. psRCH2: The Only Within-Metal Counter Ion Comparison

text: As literature context, the report cites Danilova et al. (2020) for a 2.5-fold CuSO₄-versus-CuCl₂ toxicity difference at 0.5 M; it contrasts this with typical random barcode transposon sequencing (RB-TnSeq) concentrations of 0.05–2 mM and infers smaller counter-ion effects there.
quote: - **Danilova et al. (2020)** reported 2.5-fold differences between CuSO₄ and CuCl₂ toxicity at 0.5 M — a concentration range where osmotic effects dominate. At the lower concentrations used in RB-TnSeq (typically 0.05–2 mM), counter ion effects would be proportionally smaller, consistent with our finding that counter ions are negligible for genome-wide fitness.
heading: Literature Context

heading: Novel Contribution

text: NaCl is not a chloride-only control because it introduces Na⁺ and osmotic stress; KCl or choline chloride would isolate chloride more specifically, although available choline chloride experiments differ in concentration.
quote: - **NaCl ≠ pure Cl⁻ control**: NaCl delivers both Na⁺ and Cl⁻. The NaCl fitness profile includes sodium toxicity and osmotic stress effects beyond just chloride. A pure KCl or choline chloride control would more specifically isolate chloride effects (some FB organisms have choline chloride experiments but at different concentrations).
heading: Limitations

text: The 39.8% overlap depends on the NaCl-importance rule, fit < -1 or n_sick ≥ 1; changing its stringency would change the overlap.
quote: - **Threshold sensitivity**: The 39.8% overlap depends on the NaCl-importance threshold (fit < -1 or n_sick ≥ 1). A stricter threshold would reduce overlap; a more permissive one would increase it.
heading: Limitations

text: Approximately 14.3% of protein-coding genes, considered putative essentials, lacked transposon insertions and were absent from both fitness datasets; these genes were 82% core.
quote: - **Essential genes excluded**: ~14.3% of protein-coding genes (putative essentials) lack transposon insertions and are absent from both NaCl and metal fitness data. These are 82% core; their exclusion affects both the original and corrected conservation analyses equally.
heading: Limitations

text: Manganese, cadmium, selenium, mercury, iron, molybdenum, and tungsten were each tested in only one organism, DvH, so their overlap statistics lack cross-organism replication.
